report:
The evidence does **not** clearly support ginkgo extract as an effective treatment for tinnitus, despite some promising smaller studies.

**What the research shows:**

- **Cochrane systematic review (updated 2022):** The most authoritative assessment, pooling multiple randomized controlled trials, concluded that "there is uncertainty about the benefits and harms of Ginkgo biloba for the treatment of tinnitus when compared to placebo" and that the certainty of evidence is low. The earlier 2013 version stated the limited evidence "did not demonstrate that Ginkgo biloba was effective for tinnitus." ([Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003852_ginkgo-biloba-tinnitus); [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36383762/))

- **Largest trial (Drew & Davies, BMJ 2001):** This double-blind, placebo-controlled trial—the largest to date—found no effect of 150 mg/day ginkgo extract on tinnitus symptoms. ([Tinnitus UK](https://tinnitus.org.uk/tinnitus-treatments/ginkgo-biloba/))

- **One favorable systematic review (von Boetticher, 2011):** A review of trials using the standardized extract EGb 761® concluded it was an "evidence-based treatment option," but this analysis has been criticized for including smaller, lower-quality studies. ([PMC/NIH](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157487/))

- **Clinical consensus:** Multiple clinical sources note that trials "consistently show no benefit over placebo" and that current clinical guidelines do not support ginkgo for tinnitus. ([Treble Health](https://treblehealth.com/ginkgo-biloba-and-tinnitus/); [Ear Labs](https://earlabs.app/articles/ginkgo-biloba-tinnitus-evidence/))

**Bottom line:** While a few smaller studies suggest possible benefit for a specific standardized extract, the highest-quality evidence—the Cochrane review and the largest individual trial—finds no convincing benefit beyond placebo. Ginkgo also carries potential side effects (e.g., bleeding risk). The answer is likely **no**, or at best, unproven.
